glossary.plain: Reinforced Cement Concrete: concrete with steel bars (sariya) inside. Your flat's skeleton (pillars, beams, slabs) is RCC. Never break or drill big holes into RCC without an engineer's OK.
A vertical RCC post that carries the building's weight down to the ground. Never cut or chip it. In Room 1 there is a 9" pillar at the north-west corner.
A horizontal RCC member that runs between pillars just under the ceiling, often showing as a 'drop' in the ceiling. Carries the slab. Never cut it.
The flat RCC plate that forms your ceiling and the floor of the flat above. About 5–6" thick.
Most walls between pillars are just 'filler' walls made of red bricks or AAC blocks, then plastered. 9" for outer walls, 4.5" for inner ones. You can cut these for switches and pipes (not RCC).
A light, large grey building block used instead of red bricks. Easier to cut, insulates better.

In Room 1's south wall, one 7'3" long part sticks 3'4" into the room, so that part of the wall is 3'4" deep instead of normal thickness. It's solid (not a cupboard). Such thick blocks usually wrap a pillar, a shaft for pipes/wires, or the building's structure — ask the builder before cutting into it. The designs use its face for a study desk / dresser.
A 12–15 mm layer of cement and sand spread on bricks to make walls flat. Builders usually hand over walls already plastered (often with one coat of white putty/paint).
An opening is the hole left in a wall for a door or window. A lintel is the small concrete beam over the opening that carries the wall above.

White paste (cement or acrylic based) spread in 2 thin coats (about 1–1.5 mm) on plaster and sanded smooth. It fills pores and small cracks so paint looks smooth. Used only indoors, on walls and ceiling — not waterproof, so never on outside walls. e.g. Birla White WallCare, JK WallMaxx (about ₹30–45 per kg).
A first thin coat that makes paint stick and use less paint. Goes on after putty and before the colour coats (water-based interior wall primer).

Normal water-based wall paint, 2 coats over primer. Three grades (Asian Paints example, 2026 prices for 20 L): economy Tractor Emulsion ~₹212/L, standard Apcolite Premium ~₹437/L, luxury Royale ~₹764/L. Costlier grades are more washable and smoother. Berger, Nerolac and Dulux have similar ranges.
The cheapest chalky wall paint. Marks easily and can't be washed; mostly avoided in bedrooms now.
A soft, cloudy-looking lime-based wall finish. Gives a hand-made textured look. Used on the accent wall in Options A and C.

One wall painted or panelled differently from the others to make it the room's focus, usually the wall behind the bed. In Option D it's the east (bed) wall painted terracotta, the other walls warm white.
A warm brownish-orange, the colour of baked clay pots (matka / kulhad). Calm and earthy; pairs well with white, indigo, cane and wood.
Deep blue from the indigo plant, classic in Indian block-print textiles. Used for Option D's cotton curtains.
Greige = grey + beige (DEFAULT's floor). Sage = soft grey-green (DEFAULT's headboard and curtains). Teal = deep blue-green (Option C's accent wall).
Boards fixed on a wall (fluted, slatted, fabric or cane) for looks and a bit of sound softening. Costs much more than paint.
Plaster of Paris. Used for smooth ceiling finishing, cornices and older-style false ceilings. Gypsum board has mostly replaced POP false ceilings.

A second ceiling hung below the concrete slab using steel channels and gypsum boards. Hides wires, gives space for hidden (cove) lights and recessed downlights. A 'band' or 'peripheral' false ceiling covers only the edges of the room.
12.5 mm white board (Gyproc etc.) screwed to a steel frame to make a false ceiling or partition. Joints are taped, puttied and painted, so it looks like a normal ceiling.
A hidden LED strip tucked in a groove of the false ceiling (or on a pelmet), so you see a soft glow on the ceiling but not the light itself.
A box or board above the curtains that hides the curtain rod or track. In Option D it's a laminated plywood box with an LED strip on top.
A 3–4" strip at the bottom of the walls (tile, wood or aluminium) that protects the paint from mops and feet.

The most common Indian floor today. Made from clay, quartz, feldspar and silica, pressed and fired at about 1,200 °C, so it becomes dense and glass-like: hard, low water absorption, doesn't stain easily. Cheaper and easier to keep than marble. GVT/PGVT = glazed with a printed design (can look like marble, wood or terrazzo). Brands: Kajaria, Somany, Johnson, Nitco.

Indian Patent Stone: a smooth grey cement-concrete floor. Some builders hand over flats with IPS or a rough cement screed so owners can choose tiles. It works, but it's dusty and cold-looking — most people tile over it.
A denser, premium kind of vitrified tile, often in big slabs (1200×1200 mm or more). Used in Option B.
Natural stone (e.g. Makrana white). Beautiful but porous: it stains, needs polishing and costs more. None of the designs use marble, to keep cost and upkeep down.
Hard natural stone, very durable. Used for window sills and door thresholds (black granite) in these designs, not for the whole floor.
A green-grey natural stone from Rajasthan, cheap, tough and cool underfoot. 'Leather finish' = matte textured surface. Used in Option C's balcony.
A floor with chips of stone set in cement and polished. The options use 'terrazzo-look' tiles (vitrified tiles printed to look like terrazzo).
Vitrified tile printed and textured like wooden planks. Looks warm, but you can mop it like tile. Used in Option A.
The filler in the gaps between tiles. Epoxy grout is stain-proof and colour-matched; cement grout is cheaper but darkens over time.
What the tile sits on: a 1:4 cement-sand bed about 40–50 mm thick, or a thin layer of tile adhesive on an already-level floor.
The stone strip at the bottom of a doorway. At the balcony it also steps down and slopes away so rainwater doesn't come in.
Outdoor tile with a rough surface so it isn't slippery when wet. R11 is a slip-resistance rating.
A chemical coating under balcony and bathroom floors so water doesn't leak to the flat below. Needs a slope (fall) towards the drain.
A flat woven cotton or jute rug (Panipat, Jaipur). Cheap, washable, very Indian.
Madhubani: folk painting from Bihar (Option D's framed print). Moodha: a round cane stool. Jaali: a carved lattice screen (Option C).
Thin wooden sheets glued in layers into an 18 mm board. MR = moisture resistant (fine for dry rooms), BWR/BWP = boiling-water resistant/proof (for damp areas, costlier).
High Density High Moisture Resistance board: a pressed fibre board that's harder and cheaper than good plywood and handles humidity well. Popular for wardrobes now.
Cheaper pressed-wood boards. MDF is smooth (good for carving/flutes); particle board is the cheapest, used in ready-made furniture and 'engineered wood'.
The box/body of a wardrobe or cabinet (sides, back, shelves), without the doors.
Carpenter's word for a cupboard door.
The storage box above the wardrobe, up to the ceiling, for suitcases and quilts.
A 0.8–1 mm printed plastic sheet glued on the board (wood-grain, white, colours). Tough, easy to clean and the most economical finish.
A real-wood slice (about 0.5 mm) glued on the board, then polished with PU. Looks like real wood, costs more than laminate.
Premium door finishes: PU is a paint-like polish, acrylic is a glossy sheet, lacquered glass is back-painted glass. Costlier than laminate.
A hinge with a small damper so the door closes gently instead of banging. Hettich / Hafele / Ebco are common brands.
The recessed base under a wardrobe or bed so you can mop under the front and your toes don't hit it.
The common, economical aluminium window/door section in India (27 mm series). Slides on tracks. Good value; slimmer 'system' windows cost more.
Plastic (vinyl) window frames with steel inside. Seals well against dust, noise and rain; white is the standard colour. Used in Option A.
Panels move sideways on 2 or 3 tracks. 3-track lets you have 2 glass panels + 1 mosquito-mesh panel. Doesn't swing into the room, so nothing gets in its way.
A window that opens on hinges like a door (inward or outward). Seals better than sliding. Inward ones need space in front.
A European casement that can tilt at the top for air or swing fully inward to clean. Used in Option B.
Panels fold like an accordion and stack at one side, opening almost the whole width. Used in Option C's balcony.
Glass heat-treated to be about 5× stronger; if it breaks it shatters into small blunt pieces. Standard for doors.
Two glass sheets with a plastic film between. If it cracks, it stays in place, so it can replace a grill.
Glass with a thin coating that keeps out heat from the sun. Keeps rooms cooler; costs more.
A fine net panel or pleated screen so you can keep the window/door open without insects.
Metal bars outside the window glass for safety. 'Invisible grill' = thin steel cables, used in Option B.
The ledge at the bottom of a window. Inside it's often granite; outside it slopes and has a drip groove so rain drips off instead of running down the wall.
A small round ceiling light pointing down. 'Recessed' ones sit inside a false ceiling; 'surface' ones are screwed onto a plain ceiling (Option D).
A flexible tape of small LEDs (sold per metre) that needs a 'driver' (power adapter). Used for cove, pelmet, wardrobe and headboard glows.
How warm or cool light looks: 2700K is warm yellow (cosy, bedrooms), 3000K warm white, 4000K neutral, 6500K cool blue-white (offices).
A rating that means a light is dust-tight and safe in rain, needed outdoors on the balcony.
A light hanging from the ceiling on a cord.

ui.title: Learn
ui.bare: This model is the bare architecture (no interior design), so there are no finishes to explain. Pick DEFAULT, A, B, C or D under Interior design, or open How homes are built.
ui.lead: You're looking at {d}. Each card says what you'll see, what it's made of (the layers from the structure up to what you touch) and where it goes. Show me flies to it; See pictures opens real photos.
ui.stepslead: The usual order for doing up one room. Each step has to finish before the next, or work gets damaged and redone.
ui.stepsnote: For Option D (budget), steps 2, 5 and 6 are skipped: no civil work, no false ceiling, no new floor.
ui.comparelead: The same room, five ways, in plain words.

svg.wallcap: the wall: bricks, then plaster + putty + paint on the room side

p: Your building stands on an RCC frame (concrete with steel bars): pillars (columns) go up, beams run between them under the ceiling, and a flat slab sits on top — your ceiling and the next flat's floor.
The walls between the pillars are brick or block 'filler' walls. They don't hold the building up, which is why you can cut small grooves in them for wires, but never in pillars, beams or the slab.

ul: Thick ("raised") wall: on the south side, one 7'3" part of the wall is 3'4" deep. It's solid, like a big block, not a cupboard. The designs put the study desk / dresser on its face. Ask the builder what's inside before drilling deep (often a pillar or a pipe/wire shaft).
Alcove: the 5'4" × 3'4" pocket next to it, perfect for a wardrobe, so the wardrobe takes no floor space from the room.
Balcony opening: the whole west side (10'5") opens to the balcony; there's no gate or frame yet, which is why every design adds a glass door.
9" pillar at the north-west corner where the opening ends.

basics.h: 3 · What's on a wall, a floor and a ceiling
stacks: Tile (vitrified) or stone, grout in the joints
notes: Which side gets putty and paint? Only the inside faces of the room's walls and the ceiling. Outside faces of outer walls get exterior paint from the building (putty isn't waterproof, so it's never used outside). The balcony's walls get exterior-grade paint, no putty.

floorpaint.h: What is your floor made of?
p: Under every floor is the concrete slab. On it the mason lays a cement-sand bed (~40–50 mm) to make it level, and on that the tiles or stone, with grout filling the joints. So it's never 'just cement' — unless the builder left an IPS (smooth grey cement) floor for you to tile.

The designs use vitrified tiles, not marble. A vitrified tile is made of clay, quartz, feldspar and silica, pressed and fired at about 1,200 °C until it turns dense and glass-like — hard, hardly absorbs water, doesn't stain. Marble is natural stone: beautiful but porous, needs polishing and costs more.
table: Fired clay-and-glass tile, printed or plain
Whatever the builder laid (usually vitrified tile)
Only if the builder left it — then add tiles

p: Walls and ceiling get the same 4 layers: putty (2 coats) → primer (1 coat) → emulsion paint (2 coats). What changes between designs is the paint grade and colour. Prices below are Asian Paints 20-litre rates (2026); Berger, Nerolac and Dulux have matching ranges at similar prices.
table: Wall putty (Birla White WallCare, JK WallMaxx)
notes: How much? Room 1 has about 590 sq ft of wall + ceiling. A litre of emulsion covers roughly 100–120 sq ft per coat, so 2 coats need about 10–12 litres.

Terracotta accent wall? Terracotta is the warm brown-orange of a clay pot (matka / kulhad). Pick a terracotta or brick-red shade from the shop's colour fan deck, buy a small sample pot and paint a 2'×2' patch first — colours look different on the wall and at night.

steps: Fix the layout, the finishes and the budget first. Changes later cost double.
Breaking / building walls, making openings. Never touch pillars, beams or the slab without an engineer.
Frames go in before the final putty so the edges can be finished neatly.
Wires in pipes (conduits) cut into the brick walls: switch boards, light points, AC point. Done before putty and flooring.
Steel channels + gypsum boards, with holes for downlights and a groove for the cove LED.
Tiles laid on a cement bed; left to set 2–3 days; skirting fixed. Cover it with sheets afterwards.
Walls and ceiling: 2 coats of putty, sanding, primer. Dusty work, so before carpentry is finished.
Wardrobe, loft, study wall, pelmet. Usually 1–2 weeks for one room.
2 coats of colour after the carpentry dust is gone. Touch-ups at the very end.
Lights, switches, fan, LED strips and drivers.
Window glass & mesh shutters, curtain rods, bed, mattress, rugs, plants.
Acid-free cleaning of tiles, remove paint spots, then move in.
